content: Mansonella streptocerca, previously known as Diptalonema streptocerca, is a parasitic roundworm that infects humans and causes the disease streptocerciasis. This parasite is commonly found in the skin of humans living in the rainforests of Africa and is also believed to infect chimpanzees. It is one of three filarial nematodes responsible for subcutaneous filariasis in humans, alongside Loa loa (the African eye worm) and Onchocerca volvulus (the causative agent of river blindness). Mansonella streptocerca is distributed across West and Central Africa. The life cycle of Mansonella streptocerca involves two hosts: a midge (genus Culicoides) and a human. The cycle begins when a midge takes a blood meal from an infected human, allowing third-stage filarial larvae to enter the bite wound. Once inside the dermis, the larvae mature into adult worms, typically residing less than 1 mm beneath the skin's surface. Female worms can grow up to 27 mm in length, while males are approximately 50 μm in diameter. The adult worms produce nonperiodic microfilariae, which primarily inhabit the skin but can also circulate in peripheral blood. These microfilariae are ingested by a midge during its blood meal. Within the midge, the microfilariae migrate to the midgut, pass through the hemocoel, and reach the thoracic muscles, where they develop into first-stage larvae and subsequently into infective third-stage larvae. These larvae then travel to the midge’s proboscis, enabling transmission to another human host during the next blood meal. Mansonella streptocerca has been reported in various regions of West and Central Africa, including Western Uganda, the Uganda-Zaire border, and the Bundibugyo district. The adult form of Mansonella streptocerca was first identified by Dr. Wayne M. Meyers during his work as a medical missionary in Africa. A distinguishing feature of the adult worm is its bent posterior end, which resembles a shepherd’s crook. This morphological characteristic allows laboratory workers to differentiate Mansonella streptocerca from other roundworm species. Infections with Mansonella streptocerca are typically asymptomatic but may occasionally cause mild dermatitis, particularly on the thorax and shoulders. Unlike Onchocerca volvulus infections, Mansonella streptocerca does not cause nodules, significant skin disease, or ocular infections. The absence of nodules makes it easier to distinguish Mansonella streptocerca infections from those caused by Onchocerca volvulus. Treatment for streptocerciasis includes the use of diethylcarbamazine (DEC), which has been reported to be effective against both the microfilarial and adult stages of Mansonella streptocerca. However, its efficacy as a definitive treatment has not been conclusively proven. Ivermectin, a common antiparasitic drug, is not considered an effective treatment for streptocerciasis. Furthermore, ivermectin is not recommended for mass treatment in areas where Mansonella streptocerca is the only endemic filarial parasite, as the side effects of the drug often outweigh the consequences of the infection itself. Preventative measures include the use of insect repellents such as DEET to protect against midge bites when traveling to endemic areas.
